checklist.whatToLookFor: Drive by and photograph the site. Look for TABC 60-day signs, plat or variance notice signs, fencing, dumpsters, utility disconnections, and survey stakes.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage. Posted signs can appear before records show up online.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search by Legal Description (Block + Subdivision keyword) and owner/buyer names for deeds, deeds of trust (naming the lender), and memorandums of contract.
checklist.typicalTiming: Deeds usually record within days of closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up each LLC or trade entity across TX Comptroller, Bizapedia, Google Search (if no franchise tax), and SOSDirect to find officers and related entities.
checklist.typicalTiming: As soon as a new entity name surfaces.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the 13-digit HCAD account number to confirm the owner of record, legal description, and changes to land use, value, or improvements.
checklist.typicalTiming: Owner updates lag the deed by weeks to months.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and trade names for pending or issued permits. TABC applications often reveal the operator LLC and DBA.
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search DSHS consumable hemp licenses by entity LLC name, DBA/trade name, or officer name (portal searches by name, not street address).
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up 8-digit permit project numbers (from Houston Sold Permits) in ILMS, or submit a GovQA open records request for unissued architectural plans.
checklist.typicalTiming: Most useful after closing, once an architect or engineer is engaged.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Check the Biweekly Plat & Variance Review tab and COH biweekly Plat Agenda spreadsheets (PlatTracker portal login is restricted to official roles).
checklist.typicalTiming: Can be filed before closing with the seller's consent.

checklist.typicalTiming: Design phase, usually after closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and entity names for regulated-entity records, such as construction stormwater coverage or storage tanks.
checklist.typicalTiming: Shortly before construction.

checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage, especially while the building is vacant.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified street address, owner, and buyer names for published legal notices, such as TABC application notices.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Drive by and photograph the site. Look for TABC 60-day signs, plat or variance notice signs, fencing, dumpsters, utility disconnections, and survey stakes.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage. Posted signs can appear before records show up online.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search by Legal Description (Block + Subdivision keyword) and owner/buyer names for deeds, deeds of trust (naming the lender), and memorandums of contract.
checklist.typicalTiming: Deeds usually record within days of closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up each LLC or trade entity across TX Comptroller, Bizapedia, Google Search (if no franchise tax), and SOSDirect to find officers and related entities.
checklist.typicalTiming: As soon as a new entity name surfaces.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the 13-digit HCAD account number to confirm the owner of record, legal description, and changes to land use, value, or improvements.
checklist.typicalTiming: Owner updates lag the deed by weeks to months.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and trade names for pending or issued permits. TABC applications often reveal the operator LLC and DBA.
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search DSHS consumable hemp licenses by entity LLC name, DBA/trade name, or officer name (portal searches by name, not street address).
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up 8-digit permit project numbers (from Houston Sold Permits) in ILMS, or submit a GovQA open records request for unissued architectural plans.
checklist.typicalTiming: Most useful after closing, once an architect or engineer is engaged.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Check the Biweekly Plat & Variance Review tab and COH biweekly Plat Agenda spreadsheets (PlatTracker portal login is restricted to official roles).
checklist.typicalTiming: Can be filed before closing with the seller's consent.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search simplified addresses and DBA/facility names in TABS. Registered projects list the owner, design firm, estimated cost, and scope.
checklist.typicalTiming: Design phase, before construction starts.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search City Council public agendas on NovusAgenda for street, alley, or utility easement abandonments and TIRZ actions near the property.
checklist.typicalTiming: Design phase, usually after closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and entity names for regulated-entity records, such as construction stormwater coverage or storage tanks.
checklist.typicalTiming: Shortly before construction.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Check 311 code complaints and cross-check periodic City Dangerous Buildings (DONDB) CSV lists; notify the City coordinator if historic.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage, especially while the building is vacant.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search Houston Sold Permits by simplified address for demolition, sewer disconnect, and commercial building permits (and note 8-digit project numbers).
checklist.typicalTiming: Final weeks before work starts.

checklist.whatToLookFor: DSHS must be notified at least 10 working days before any commercial or public building is demolished or abated.
checklist.typicalTiming: At least 10 working days before demolition starts.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified street address, owner, and buyer names for published legal notices, such as TABC application notices.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Drive by and photograph the site. Look for TABC 60-day signs, plat or variance notice signs, fencing, dumpsters, utility disconnections, and survey stakes.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage. Posted signs can appear before records show up online.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search by Legal Description (Block + Subdivision keyword) and owner/buyer names for deeds, deeds of trust (naming the lender), and memorandums of contract.
checklist.typicalTiming: Deeds usually record within days of closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up each LLC or trade entity across TX Comptroller, Bizapedia, Google Search (if no franchise tax), and SOSDirect to find officers and related entities.
checklist.typicalTiming: As soon as a new entity name surfaces.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the 13-digit HCAD account number to confirm the owner of record, legal description, and changes to land use, value, or improvements.
checklist.typicalTiming: Owner updates lag the deed by weeks to months.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and trade names for pending or issued permits. TABC applications often reveal the operator LLC and DBA.
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search DSHS consumable hemp licenses by entity LLC name, DBA/trade name, or officer name (portal searches by name, not street address).
checklist.typicalTiming: After closing, once an operator has a lease or deed.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Look up 8-digit permit project numbers (from Houston Sold Permits) in ILMS, or submit a GovQA open records request for unissued architectural plans.
checklist.typicalTiming: Most useful after closing, once an architect or engineer is engaged.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Check the Biweekly Plat & Variance Review tab and COH biweekly Plat Agenda spreadsheets (PlatTracker portal login is restricted to official roles).
checklist.typicalTiming: Can be filed before closing with the seller's consent.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search simplified addresses and DBA/facility names in TABS. Registered projects list the owner, design firm, estimated cost, and scope.
checklist.typicalTiming: Design phase, before construction starts.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search City Council public agendas on NovusAgenda for street, alley, or utility easement abandonments and TIRZ actions near the property.
checklist.typicalTiming: Design phase, usually after closing.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search the simplified address and entity names for regulated-entity records, such as construction stormwater coverage or storage tanks.
checklist.typicalTiming: Shortly before construction.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Check 311 code complaints and cross-check periodic City Dangerous Buildings (DONDB) CSV lists; notify the City coordinator if historic.
checklist.typicalTiming: Any stage, especially while the building is vacant.

checklist.whatToLookFor: Search Houston Sold Permits by simplified address for demolition, sewer disconnect, and commercial building permits (and note 8-digit project numbers).
checklist.typicalTiming: Final weeks before work starts.

checklist.whatToLookFor: DSHS must be notified at least 10 working days before any commercial or public building is demolished or abated.
checklist.typicalTiming: At least 10 working days before demolition starts.

WATCH_PROP:prop-1792765948557.notes: A new gas station development has been proposed for the property. A replat application was deferred twice and then withdrawn. Council Member Martinez requested a review of the proposal against neighborhood deed restrictions. Legal Department found that the lots are restricted to residential and cannot be replatted into an unrestricted reserve. The building appears to cover 2 lots. Next steps are unknown. Reveille Park Place Neighborhood Association would like the building to remain with a community-oriented use. Joe Wilson (Glenbrook Valley president) also wants the building to remain.

WATCH_PROP:prop-1794601682485.buildingHistory: Architects Joseph Krakower and Herb Greene designed this building for the Southwestern Bell Telephone Company, and it opened in 1959. The design reflects the “American School” of architecture, a design movement that Greene helped to originate in the late 1950s. This was intended to be a modern, distinctly American building without clear references to historic architecture. The building was originally painted a uniform off-white color with some accents of turquoise mosaic tile, which are mostly painted over but still present. The building got an early version of its current two-tone paint scheme from a later tenant, the Uniroyal Tire Company, which painted the upper section black to resemble a tire tread - a clever adaptation of Greene’s detailing.

583030000039.source_citation: Fair Haven Methodist Church. Otto Woestemeyer designed a church campus master plan beginning c. 1956. Bishop Frank A. Smith laid the cornerstone for the first unit in October 1956. By 1959, 3 of 5 units had been completed. The sanctuary completed in 1967 does not match Woestemeyer's 1950s design, and the architect for the 1967 building is not listed. At least one of Woestemeyer's 1950s units is extant. Sources: Houston Post; Houston Chronicle; historicaerials.com
